  "claims": [
    {
      "id": "f1",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints available frames without waiting for readers or writers and syncs the database file if all log frames were checkpointed.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f2",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits for no database writer and for all readers to use the most recent snapshot, then checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database file.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f3",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "After checkpointing, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART waits until all readers use only the database file, ensuring that the next writer restarts the WAL from its beginning.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f4",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE adds truncation of the WAL file to zero bytes immediately before a successful return to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART behavior.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f5",
      "concept_id": "c1",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP provides access to *pnLog and *pnCkpt status while checkpointing zero frames.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f6",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "If overlapping readers always leave at least one reader active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL file grows without bound.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f7",
      "concept_id": "c2",
      "text": "Checkpoint starvation can be avoided by attempting checkpoints during reader gaps when no process is reading the database.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are \"reader gaps\": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f8",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers automatic checkpointing after a transaction commits if a database on connection D has at least N WAL frames.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f9",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "Passing N equal to zero or a negative value to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints entirely.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f10",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "Every new connection defaults to enabled automatic checkpointing with a threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT setting.",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f11",
      "concept_id": "c3",
      "text": "Automatic checkpoints and checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() use PASSIVE mode.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f12",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "Checkpoint synchronization requires syncing the WAL before transferring its content into the database and syncing the database before resetting the WAL.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f13",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "Writers sync the WAL at every commit with PRAGMA synchronous set to FULL and omit that commit-time sync with NORMAL.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "(Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.)",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f14",
      "concept_id": "c4",
      "text": "Omitting synchronization of WAL content to disk sacrifices durability following power loss or hard reboot.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Further, syncing the content to the disk is not required, as long as the application is willing to sacrifice durability following a power loss or hard reboot.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f15",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "If another process is already checkpointing, checkpoint-lock contention returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the configured busy handler.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f16",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE also obtain an exclusive writer lock.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive \"writer\" lock on the database file.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f17",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "If the busy handler returns 0 before writer-lock acquisition or while waiting for readers, the checkpoint falls back to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f18",
      "concept_id": "c5",
      "text": "The documented busy-handler fallback to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE returns SQLITE_BUSY.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f19",
      "concept_id": "c6",
      "text": "A reader's end mark remains unchanged throughout its transaction, preserving a single database snapshot.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "But for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f20",
      "concept_id": "c6",
      "text": "A checkpoint running alongside readers must stop upon reaching a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f21",
      "concept_id": "c7",
      "text": "By default, the thread performing the COMMIT that crosses the WAL size limit also runs the automatic checkpoint.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f22",
      "concept_id": "c7",
      "text": "Under default automatic scheduling, COMMIT operations that trigger checkpoints can be much slower than other commits.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f23",
      "concept_id": "c7",
      "text": "Applications can disable automatic checkpointing and run periodic checkpoints in a separate thread or process.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "If that effect is undesirable, then the application can disable automatic checkpointing and run the periodic checkpoints in a separate thread, or separate process.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f24",
      "concept_id": "c8",
      "text": "Read performance deteriorates as the WAL grows because readers must check a larger WAL for content.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content and the time needed to check the WAL file is proportional to the size of the WAL file.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f25",
      "concept_id": "c8",
      "text": "Infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes while allowing a larger WAL.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently and let the WAL grow as large as possible before each checkpoint.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f26",
      "concept_id": "c9",
      "text": "A checkpoint normally recycles the WAL by starting overwrites at its beginning without truncating the file.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f27",
      "concept_id": "c10",
      "text": "For a successful checkpoint of one named WAL database, a non-NULL pnLog receives the total number of WAL frames.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If pnLog is not NULL, then *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f28",
      "concept_id": "c10",
      "text": "For a successful checkpoint of one named WAL database, a non-NULL pnCkpt receives the total checkpointed frame count, including frames checkpointed before the call.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If pnCkpt is not NULL,then *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f29",
      "concept_id": "c11",
      "text": "A WAL checkpoint transfers transactions from the WAL file back into the database.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a \" checkpoint \".",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f30",
      "concept_id": "c12",
      "text": "Registering a callback with sqlite3_wal_hook() disables automatic checkpointing configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().",
      "source_id": "S3",
      "quote": "Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f31",
      "concept_id": "c13",
      "text": "The WAL cannot reset during a write transaction, allowing a large write transaction to produce a large WAL file.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f32",
      "concept_id": "c14",
      "text": "When zDb is NULL or empty, checkpoint dispatch covers all attached WAL databases and leaves *pnLog and *pnCkpt undefined.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f33",
      "concept_id": "c14",
      "text": "During dispatch across attached WAL databases, SQLITE_BUSY permits attempts on the remaining databases and is returned at the end.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If an SQLITE_BUSY error is encountered when processing one or more of the attached WAL databases, the operation is still attempted on any remaining attached databases and SQLITE_BUSY is returned at the end.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f34",
      "concept_id": "c14",
      "text": "An error other than SQLITE_BUSY during attached-database processing abandons further processing and returns that error immediately.",
      "source_id": "S2",
      "quote": "If any other error occurs while processing an attached database, processing is abandoned and the error code is returned to the caller immediately.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f35",
      "concept_id": "c15",
      "text": "After a crash or ROLLBACK, rollback-journal recovery restores original database content from the rollback journal.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "In the event of a crash or ROLLBACK , the original content contained in the rollback journal is played back into the database file to revert the database file to its original state.",
      "pass": 0
    },
    {
      "id": "f36",
      "concept_id": "c16",
      "text": "The wal-index's shared-memory requirement confines readers to one machine and prevents this WAL implementation from working on a network filesystem.",
      "source_id": "S1",
      "quote": "The wal-index greatly improves the performance of readers, but the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.",
      "pass": 0
    }
  ],
  "passes": [
    {
      "pass": 0,
      "new_claims": 36,
      "total_claims": 36,
      "new_information_rate": 1.0
    }
  ],
  "handoffs": [],
  "verdict": "BOUNDED-STAGE",
  "limitations": [
    "Novelty is assessed only against the supplied inventory of SQLite, transactions and write-ahead logging; those names do not establish detailed mechanism coverage.",
    "The parent neighborhood adds no missing concept because the supported immediate parent domains are already inventoried.",
    "The frontier neighborhood is empty because the packet establishes no emerging development from the last 12–18 months.",
    "Reasons report the five 0–5 axis scores and their supplied weighted CVS; selection uses threshold 3.2 and the stated hard gates.",
    "Viability scores are packet-bounded and capped at 3 because the three documents share one publisher; RESEARCH denotes selection for further research, not completion of full /dr source requirements.",
    "S1 says RESTART and TRUNCATE may block readers, while S2 says RESTART does not impede readers and defines TRUNCATE through RESTART; the packet does not resolve that difference, and mode claims follow S2.",
    "S1's application-initiated overview lists three modes and mentions RESET, while S2 documents five SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_* modes; introduction dates and the history behind this mismatch are unsupported.",
    "One packet-bounded pass does not establish conceptual saturation or empirical performance results."
  ]
}

claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: If overlapping readers always leave at least one reader active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL file grows without bound.
claims.quote: if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Checkpoint starvation can be avoided by attempting checkpoints during reader gaps when no process is reading the database.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers automatic checkpointing after a transaction commits if a database on connection D has at least N WAL frames.
claims.quote: causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing N equal to zero or a negative value to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint disables automatic checkpoints entirely.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Every new connection defaults to enabled automatic checkpointing with a threshold of 1000 pages or the SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT setting.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Automatic checkpoints and checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.text: Checkpoint synchronization requires syncing the WAL before transferring its content into the database and syncing the database before resetting the WAL.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: Writers sync the WAL at every commit with PRAGMA synchronous set to FULL and omit that commit-time sync with NORMAL.
claims.quote: (Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.)

claims.text: Omitting synchronization of WAL content to disk sacrifices durability following power loss or hard reboot.
claims.quote: Further, syncing the content to the disk is not required, as long as the application is willing to sacrifice durability following a power loss or hard reboot.

claims.text: If another process is already checkpointing, checkpoint-lock contention returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the configured busy handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked in this case.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE also obtain an exclusive writer lock.
claims.quote: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock on the database file.

claims.text: If the busy handler returns 0 before writer-lock acquisition or while waiting for readers, the checkpoint falls back to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: The documented busy-handler fallback to SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further. SQLITE_BUSY is returned in this case.

claims.text: A reader's end mark remains unchanged throughout its transaction, preserving a single database snapshot.
claims.quote: But for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.

claims.text: A checkpoint running alongside readers must stop upon reaching a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: By default, the thread performing the COMMIT that crosses the WAL size limit also runs the automatic checkpoint.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: Under default automatic scheduling, COMMIT operations that trigger checkpoints can be much slower than other commits.
claims.quote: This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

claims.text: Applications can disable automatic checkpointing and run periodic checkpoints in a separate thread or process.
claims.quote: If that effect is undesirable, then the application can disable automatic checkpointing and run the periodic checkpoints in a separate thread, or separate process.

claims.text: Read performance deteriorates as the WAL grows because readers must check a larger WAL for content.
claims.quote: read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content and the time needed to check the WAL file is proportional to the size of the WAL file.

claims.text: Infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes while allowing a larger WAL.
claims.quote: To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently and let the WAL grow as large as possible before each checkpoint.

claims.text: A checkpoint normally recycles the WAL by starting overwrites at its beginning without truncating the file.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: For a successful checkpoint of one named WAL database, a non-NULL pnLog receives the total number of WAL frames.
claims.quote: If pnLog is not NULL, then *pnLog is set to the total number of frames in the log file

claims.text: For a successful checkpoint of one named WAL database, a non-NULL pnCkpt receives the total checkpointed frame count, including frames checkpointed before the call.
claims.quote: If pnCkpt is not NULL,then *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: A WAL checkpoint transfers transactions from the WAL file back into the database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: Registering a callback with sqlite3_wal_hook() disables automatic checkpointing configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: The WAL cannot reset during a write transaction, allowing a large write transaction to produce a large WAL file.
claims.quote: the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL file.

claims.text: When zDb is NULL or empty, checkpoint dispatch covers all attached WAL databases and leaves *pnLog and *pnCkpt undefined.
claims.quote: zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db. In this case the values written to output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt are undefined.

claims.text: During dispatch across attached WAL databases, SQLITE_BUSY permits attempts on the remaining databases and is returned at the end.
claims.quote: If an SQLITE_BUSY error is encountered when processing one or more of the attached WAL databases, the operation is still attempted on any remaining attached databases and SQLITE_BUSY is returned at the end.

claims.text: An error other than SQLITE_BUSY during attached-database processing abandons further processing and returns that error immediately.
claims.quote: If any other error occurs while processing an attached database, processing is abandoned and the error code is returned to the caller immediately.

claims.text: After a crash or ROLLBACK, rollback-journal recovery restores original database content from the rollback journal.
claims.quote: In the event of a crash or ROLLBACK , the original content contained in the rollback journal is played back into the database file to revert the database file to its original state.

claims.text: The wal-index's shared-memory requirement confines readers to one machine and prevents this WAL implementation from working on a network filesystem.
claims.quote: The wal-index greatly improves the performance of readers, but the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.
